challenges.name: dto-whitelist-runtime
challenges.title: What a DTO type does at runtime
challenges.description: Two statements on the PATCH /users/me/profile incident: what a TypeScript cast does to the request body, and what ValidationPipe does with a property the DTO does not declare.

questions.explanation: False. A type assertion only tells the compiler what shape to assume; TypeScript erases it, and the emitted JavaScript is `return { ok: true, dto: input }`. The object passed to the repository is the parsed request body with every key the client sent, and the repository writes every key it receives - which is exactly what the audit log shows. To remove fields, code has to build a new object from the allowed fields (or ValidationPipe with whitelist has to strip them). The misconception is that TypeScript types filter or check data at runtime; they never run.

True. With whitelist: true, ValidationPipe treats every property without a validation decorator as not allowed; forbidNonWhitelisted: true turns that into an error instead of silently stripping it. The pipe runs before the handler, so the request ends with 400 and a message array containing "property isAdmin should not exist", and updateProfile() is never called. With whitelist: true alone, isAdmin would be stripped and the request would succeed with only displayName. The misconception is that declaring a DTO class is enough: the global pipe options decide what happens to unknown properties.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-profile-whitelist
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: a DTO that lets unknown fields through
challenges.description: An AI assistant was asked: "Write the request validation for PATCH /users/me/profile. UpdateProfileDto has three optional fields: displayName (string, 1-50 characters), bio (string, at most 280 characters) and avatarUrl (https URL, at most 2048 characters). Return 400 with the list of messages when the body is invalid, otherwise pass the DTO to UsersRepository.updateProfile()." Its validateUpdateProfile() checks the three fields and its tests passed. A week later a learner had 9,999,999 EXP on the leaderboard and admin rights, both set through this endpoint. Fix validateUpdateProfile() so that only displayName, bio and avatarUrl can ever reach the repository. A body with any other own property is rejected with 400 and one message per unknown property, "property <name> should not exist", in the order the properties appear in the body, followed by the field messages in the order displayName, bio, avatarUrl. Keep the existing rules and messages for the three fields and for a body that is not a JSON object. Input: { "userId": "u1", "body": "<raw JSON text of the request body>" }. Output: the response status and messages, what the repository received, and the stored user row, as printed by the test runner. The public tests pass on the assistant's code; the hidden tests send what an attacker would send.
hints: The validator checks displayName, bio and avatarUrl. What happens to a fourth property in the body - which object does the function return, and what does the repository do with it?
Look at the last line of validateUpdateProfile() and at the `as UpdateProfileDto` cast. Does a cast change the object at runtime? Then look at how UsersRepository.updateProfile() copies the changes.

A similar case: validating { title, price } for a product. `Object.keys(input).filter((key) => !['title', 'price'].includes(key))` lists the keys to reject, and `const product = {}; if (typeof input.title === 'string') product.title = input.title;` builds a new object instead of returning the input. An array lookup does not see inherited names such as toString, while `key in { title: true }` does.
